label: sec:reg-uni
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $G^{\text{uni}}$ be the set of unipotent elements in $G$. By \cite[Theorem 6.6]{Lu94}, $$G^{\text{uni}} \cap G_{\geqslant 0}=\bigsqcup_{w_1, w_2 \in W; \operatorname{supp}(w_1) \cap \operatorname{supp}(w_2)=\emptyset} U^+_{w_1, >0} U^-_{w_2, >0}.$$ 

Suppose that $G$ is almost simple. Let $w_1, w_2 \in W$ and $g \in U^+_{w_1, >0} U^-_{w_2, >0}$. Let $J_i=\operatorname{supp}(w_i)$ for $i=1, 2$. We assume furthermore that $J_1 \cap J_2=\emptyset$. Then $\dot w_{J_2} g \dot w_{J_2} ^{-1} \in U^+$. 
If $J_2\neq \emptyset$ and $J_2 \neq I$, then there exists $i \in I-J_2$ such that in the Dynkin diagram of $G$, the vertex corresponds $i$ is connected to some vertex in $J_2$. In this case, $w_{J_2}(\Phi_{J_1}) \cap \Phi_{\{i\}}=\emptyset$ and $\dot w_{J_2} g \dot w_{J_2} ^{-1} \in U_{P^+_{I-\{i\}}}$. Hence $g$ is not regular. 

Similarly, if $J_1 \neq \emptyset$ and $J_1 \neq I$, then $g$ is not regular. It is obvious that if $J_1=J_2=\emptyset$, then $g=1$ and hence is not regular. Finally if $(J_1, J_2)=(I, \emptyset)$ or $(\emptyset, I)$, then $g$ is regular. 

The ``in particular'' part follows from that the fact that $\sqcup_{w \in W, \operatorname{supp}(w)=I} U^\pm_{w, >0}$ is connected and dense in $U^\pm$.
head: environment

label: main1
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{main1}
Let $w_1, w_2 \in W$. Then 

(1) $G_{w_1, w_2, >0} \cap G^{{\mathrm{reg}}, \text{ss}} \neq \emptyset$. 

(2) $G_{w_1, w_2, >0} \subset G^{{\mathrm{reg}}, \text{ss}}$ if and only if $\operatorname{supp}(w_1)=\operatorname{supp}(w_2)=I$.  

(3) Suppose that $G$ is almost simple. Then $G_{w_1, w_2, >0} \subset G^{{\mathrm{reg}}}$ if and only if $\operatorname{supp}(w_1)=I$ or $\operatorname{supp}(w_2)=I$.
head: environment

label: lem:w-to-1
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:w-to-1}
Let $g$ be an oscillatory element. Then there exists a unique element $u \in U^-_{>0}$ such that $u ^{-1} g u \in B^+$. Moreover, $g=u u' t u ^{-1}$ for some $u' \in U^+_{\geqslant 0}$ and $t \in T$ with $\alpha_i(t)>1$ for all $i \in I$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $\ensuremath{\mathcal {B}}\xspace=G/B^+$ be the flag variety of $G$. We denote the action of $G$ on $\ensuremath{\mathcal {B}}\xspace$ by $g \cdot B:=g B g ^{-1}$. Let $\ensuremath{\mathcal {B}}\xspace_{>0}=U^-_{>0} \cdot B^+ \subset \ensuremath{\mathcal {B}}\xspace$ be the totally positive flag manifold and $\ensuremath{\mathcal {B}}\xspace_{\geqslant 0}=\overline{\ensuremath{\mathcal {B}}\xspace_{>0}}$ be the totally nonnegative flag manifold. By \cite[Corollary 8.11]{Lu94}, there exists $B \in \ensuremath{\mathcal {B}}\xspace_{\geqslant 0}$ with $g \in B$. We have $g^m \in G_{>0}$ for $m \in \ensuremath{\mathbb {N}}\xspace$. By \cite[Lemma 8.2]{Lu94}, there exists a unique $B' \in \ensuremath{\mathcal {B}}\xspace_{\geqslant 0}$ with $g^n \in B'$. Since $g \in B$, we have $g^n \in B$. Thus $B=B'$. By \cite[Lemma 8.5]{Lu94}, $B' \in \ensuremath{\mathcal {B}}\xspace_{>0}$. Hence $B=u B^+ u ^{-1}$ for some $u \in U^-_{>0}$. So $u ^{-1} g u \in B^+$. The uniqueness of $u$ follows from the uniqueness of $B$. 

Let $u ^{-1} g u=u' t$ with $u' \in U^+$ and $t \in T$. We then have $u u' t=g u \in G_{\geqslant 0}$. Therefore we have $u' \in U^+_{\geqslant 0}$ and $t \in T_{>0}$. Moreover, $g^m=u (u' t)^m u ^{-1}=u u'_m t^m u ^{-1}$ for some $u'_m \in U^+_{>0}$. By \cite[Corollary 8.10]{Lu94}, $\alpha_i(t^m)>1$ for all $i \in I$. Hence $\alpha_i(t)>1$ for all $i \in I$.
head: environment

label: lem:root
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:root}
Suppose that $G$ is almost simple and $J, J'$ are proper subsets of $I$. Then there exists $j \notin J'$ such that $w_{J'}(\alpha_j) \notin \Phi_J$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
If $J' \subset J$, then we may take $j$ to be any vertex not in $J$. 

Now assume that $J' \not \subset J$. Set $K=J \cap J'$. Then $J'-K \neq \emptyset$. We consider $J$ as a sub-diagram of the Coxeter diagram of $I$. Let $C$ be a connected component of $J'$ that contains some vertex $j_1$ in $J'-K$. Since $J' \subsetneq I$, there exists $j \notin J'$ such that $j$ is connected to a vertex $j'$ in $C$. 

Let $\omega_{j_1}$ be the fundamental weight of $j_1$ with respect to $\Phi$ and $\omega_{J', j_1}$ be the fundamental weight of $j_1$ with respect to $\Phi_{J'}$. Then $\omega_{j_1} \in \sum_{i \in I} \ensuremath{\mathbb {Q}}\xspace_{>0} \alpha_i$ and $\omega_{J', j_1} \in \sum_{i \in C} \ensuremath{\mathbb {Q}}\xspace_{>0} \alpha_i$. Note that $w_{J'}(\omega_{J', j_1})=-\omega_{J', j_2}=\omega_{J', j_1}-(\omega_{J', j_1}+\omega_{J', j_2})$ for some $j_2 \in C$. We have $\omega_{J', j_2} \in \sum_{i \in C} \ensuremath{\mathbb {Q}}\xspace_{>0} \alpha_i$ and hence $\omega_{J', j_1}+\omega_{J', j_2} \in \sum_{i \in C} \ensuremath{\mathbb {Q}}\xspace_{>0} \alpha_i$. Since the restriction of $\omega_{j_1}$ to the root system $\Phi_{J'}$ equals to $\omega_{J', j_1}$, we have $$w_{J'}(\omega_{j_1})=\omega_{j_1}-(\omega_{J', j_1}+\omega_{J', j_2}) \in \omega_{j_1}-\sum_{i \in C} \ensuremath{\mathbb {Q}}\xspace_{>0} \alpha_i.$$

Now $\<w_{J'}(\alpha_j), \omega_{j_1}\>=\<\alpha_j, w_{J'}(\omega_{j_1})\> \in \<\alpha_j,  \omega_{j_1}-\sum_{i \in C} \ensuremath{\mathbb {Q}}\xspace_{>0} \alpha_i\>=-\<\alpha_j, \sum_{i \in C} \ensuremath{\mathbb {Q}}\xspace_{>0} \alpha_i\>$. Since $\<\alpha_j, \alpha_i\> \leqslant 0$ for any $i \in C$ and $\<\alpha_j, \alpha_{j'}\><0$, we have $\<w_{J'}(\alpha_j), \omega_{j_1}\>>0$. Since $j_1 \notin J$, we have $w_{J'}(\alpha_j) \notin \Phi_J$.
head: environment

title: Lemma
body_md: Let $1 \leqslant k \leqslant n$. Set $$V_k=\{(A_1,...,A_n)\in\ensuremath{\mathbb {R}}\xspace^n;\sum_ja_{ij}A_j=a_{kk} A_i \text{ for all }i\in[1,n]\}.$$ Then $\dim V_k=1$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
We argue by induction on $n$. 

If $n=1$, the result is obvious. 

Assume now that $n\geqslant2$. Let $c=a_{kk}$ and $I_c=\{i\in[1,n];a_{ii}=c\}$. Let $(A_1,...,A_n)\in V_k$. If $A_n=0$, then $(A_1,...,A_{n-1})$ satisfy a condition similar to that defining $V_k$. In this case, the statement follow from the induction hypothesis.

If $n\notin I_c$, then $(a_{nn}-c)A_n=0$ and $A_n=0$. 

We assume that $n\in I_c$. If $n-1\in I_c$, then $a_{n-1,n}A_n=0$. Since $a_{n-1,n}\ne0$, we have $A_n=0$ and the statement follows again from the induction hypothesis.

Now we assume that $n\in I_c,n-1\notin I_c$. If $n-2\in I_c$, then we have the linear system
\[\left\{
\begin{aligned} a_{n-2,n-1}A_{n-1}+a_{n-2,n}A_n &=0\\ (a_{n-1,n-1}-c)A_{n-1}+a_{n-1,n}A_n &=0
\end{aligned}
\right.
\]

The determinant of this linear system is
$$a_{n-2,n-1}a_{n-1,n}-(a_{n-1,n-1}-c)a_{n-2,n}=\Delta_{\{n-2, n-1\}, \{n-1, n\}}+ca_{n-2.n}>0.$$

It follows that $A_{n-1}=A_n=0$. In particular $A_n=0$ and we are done.

We then assume that $n\in I_c$, $n-1\notin I_c$, $n-2\notin I_c$. If $n-3\in I_c$, we have the linear system
\[\left\{
\begin{aligned} a_{n-3,n-2}A_{n-2}+a_{n-3,n-1}A_{n-1}+a_{n-3,n}A_n &=0\\ (a_{n-2,n-2}-c)A_{n-2}+a_{n-2,n-1}A_{n-1}+a_{n-2,n}A_n &=0 \\
(a_{n-1,n-1}-c)A_{n-1}+a_{n-1,n}A_n &=0
\end{aligned}
\right.
\]

The determinant of this system of linear equations is
\begin{align*} &a_{n-3,n-2}a_{n-2,n-1}a_{n-1,n}+(a_{n-2,n-2}-c)(a_{n-1,n-1}-c)a_{n-3,n}\\&
-a_{n-3,n-1}(a_{n-2,n-2}-c)a_{n-1,n}-a_{n-3,n-2}(a_{n-1,n-1}-c)a_{n-2,n}\\&
=
\Delta_{\{n-3, n-2, n-1\}, \{n-2, n-1, n\}}+c(\Delta_{\{n-3, n-1\}, \{n-1, n\}}+\Delta_{\{n-3, n-2\}, \{n-2, n\}})+c^2 a_{n-3,n}.
\end{align*}
Again the determinant is $>0$. It follows that $A_{n-2}=A_{n-1}=A_n=0$. In particular $A_n=0$ and we are done.

Thus we can assume $n\in I_c, n-1\notin I_c, n-2\notin I_c, n-3\notin I_c$.
Continuing in this way we see that we can assume $n\in I_c$ and  $n-1,n-2,...,1$ are not in $I_c$.

Then we can choose $A_n$ at random. From
$(a_{n-1,n-1}-c)A_{n-1}+a_{n-1,n}A_n=0$ where $a_{n-1,n-1}-c\neq 0$ we determine uniquely $A_{n-1}$.
From $(a_{n-2,n-2}-c)A_{n-2}+a_{n-2,n-1}A_{n-1}+a_{n-2,n}A_n=0$ where $a_{n-2,n-2}-c\neq 0$ we
determine uniquely $A_{n-2}$.
Continuing in this way we see that $A_{n-1},A_{n-2},...,A_1$ are uniquely determined
by $A_n$. Hence $\dim V_k=1$.
head: environment

label: lem:conj
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:conj}
Let $w \in W$ and $J=\operatorname{supp}(w)$. Then for any $t \in T_{>0}$ and $u \in U^+_{w, >0}$, there exists $u' \in U^-_{w_{t, J} ^{-1}, >0}$ such that $(u') ^{-1} t u u' \in \bar t_{J} U^+_{w, >0}$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
We prove that 

(a) {\it Let $w \in W$, $u \in U^+_{w, >0}$ and $t \in T_{>0}$. Let $i \in J$. If $\alpha_i(t)<1$, then there exists $b>0$ such that $y_i(-b) t u y_i(b) \in s_i(t) U^+_{w, >0}$.}

Let $c=\alpha_i(t)<1$. We have $\pi^+_{\{i\}}(u)=x_i(a)$ for some $a>0$. Set $b=\frac{1-c}{c a}>0$. By \cite[\S 2.11]{Lu94}, $y_i(-b) t u y_i(b) \in y_i(-b) y_i(b') t' u'$ for some $b'>0$, $t' \in T_{>0}$ and $u' \in U^+_{w, >0}$. In particular, $y_i(-b) t u y_i(b) \in P^+_{\{i\}}$. Then \begin{align*} \pi^+_{\{i\}}(y_i(-b) t u y_i(b)) &=y_i(-b) t x_i(a) y_i(b)=t y_i(-\frac{1-c}{a}) x_i(a) y_i(\frac{1-c}{ca}) \\ &=t x_i(\frac{a}{c}) \alpha_i^\vee(\frac{1}{c}).\end{align*} Note that $t \alpha_i^\vee(\frac{1}{c})=s_i(t)$. (a) is proved. 

Now the statement follows from (a) by induction on $\ell(w_{t, \operatorname{supp}(w)})$.
head: environment

title: Theorem
body_md: Let $t \in T_{>1}$ and $C$ be the regular semisimple conjugacy class of $t$ in $G$. Then $C \cap G_{>0} \neq \emptyset$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
It suffices to consider the case where that $G$ is semisimple. Let $\mathfrak g$ be the Lie algebra of $G$. For $i\in I$, let $e_i\in\mathfrak g$ (resp. $f_i\in\mathfrak g$) be the differential of $x_i$ (resp. $y_i$). Let $\mathfrak h$ be the Cartan subalgebra of $\mathfrak g$ corresponding to $T$. Let $\mathfrak h_\ensuremath{\mathbb {R}}\xspace$ be the set of real points of $\mathfrak h$ and let $\mathfrak h_+$ be the fundamental open Weyl chamber in $\mathfrak h_\ensuremath{\mathbb {R}}\xspace$. Let $\exp:\mathfrak g  
   \ifbool{@display}{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow} 
    G$ be the exponential map. By our assumption on $C$, we can find $y\in\mathfrak h_+$ such that $\exp(y)=t$.

Let $\mathfrak h/W$ be the set of orbits of the standard Weyl group action on $\mathfrak h$. For $x\in\mathfrak g$, the semisimple part of $x$ is $G$-conjugate to an element $x'\in\mathfrak h$ whose Weyl group orbit depends only on $x$; this defines a map $\ensuremath{\mathcal {I}}\xspace:\mathfrak g  
   \ifbool{@display}{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow} 
    \mathfrak h/W$. Following \cite{K}, we define the set of ``Jacobi elements'' 
$$\mathfrak g_{>0}=\{\sum_ia_if_i+h+\sum_ib_ie_i;a_i\in\ensuremath{\mathbb {R}}\xspace_{>0},b_i\in\ensuremath{\mathbb {R}}\xspace_{>0},h\in\mathfrak h_\ensuremath{\mathbb {R}}\xspace\}.$$
By \cite[(3.5.26)]{K}, we have $\ensuremath{\mathcal {I}}\xspace(\mathfrak g_{>0})=\ensuremath{\mathcal {I}}\xspace(\mathfrak h_+)$. Hence any element in $\mathfrak g_{>0}$ is regular semisimple and contained in an $\ensuremath{\mathbb {R}}\xspace$-split Cartan subalgebra and we can find $x\in\mathfrak g_{>0}$ such that the semisimple part of $x$ is $G$-conjugate to $y$; since $x$ is semisimple we see that $x$ is $G$-conjugate to $y$. Since $\exp(y)\in C$, we see that $\exp(x)\in C$. 

It remains to show that $\exp$ maps $\mathfrak g_{>0}$ into $G_{>0}$. This property is stated in \cite[5.8(c)]{Lu94} where a property close to it is proved (see \cite[5.9(c)]{Lu94}). But as mentioned in \cite[p.550, footnote]{Lu94}, a similar proof yields \cite[5.8(c)]{Lu94}.
head: environment

label: conj
title: Conjecture
head: environment

label: u-v
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{u-v}
Let $V$ be an irreducible finite dimensional representation of $G$ and $\beta$ be the canonical basis of $V$. Let $J \subset I$ and $V_J \subset V$ be the $L_J$-submodule spanned by the highest weight vector of $V$. Let $V_{\geqslant 0}=\sum_{b \in \beta} \ensuremath{\mathbb {R}}\xspace_{\geqslant 0} b$ and $(V_J)_{\geqslant 0}=V_J \cap V_{\geqslant 0}$. Then for any $w \in W^J$ and $u \in U^-_{w, >0}$, we have $$u \cdot (V_J)_{\geqslant 0}=(u \cdot V_J) \cap V_{\geqslant 0}.$$
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
By \cite[\S 3.2]{Lu94}, $u \cdot V_{\geqslant 0} \subset V_{\geqslant 0}$. Thus $u \cdot (V_J)_{\geqslant 0} \subset (u \cdot V_J) \cap V_{\geqslant 0}$. Now we prove the other direction. By definition, $(V_J)_{\geqslant 0}=\sum_{b \in \beta \cap V_J} \ensuremath{\mathbb {R}}\xspace_{\geqslant 0} b$. We recall the following result. 

(a) {\it Let $i \in I$ and $b \in \beta$ such that $x_i(a) \cdot b=b$ for all $a \in \ensuremath{\mathbb {R}}\xspace$. Then $\dot s_i \cdot b \in \beta$.}

This is a special case of the braid group action on the canonical basis \cite{Lu96}. See also \cite[Lemma 2.8]{BH}. 

Let $w=s_{i_1} \cdots s_{i_n}$ be a reduced expression. Since $w \in W^J$, for any $j$ we have $(s_{i_{j+1}} \cdots s_{i_n}) ^{-1} \alpha_{i_j} \notin \Phi_J$. By definition, $x_{i_j}(a) (s_{i_{j+1}} \cdots s_{i_n}) \cdot b=(s_{i_{j+1}} \cdots s_{i_n}) \cdot b$ for any $1 \leqslant j \leqslant n$, $a \in \ensuremath{\mathbb {R}}\xspace$ and $b \in V_J$. Thus by (a), for any $b \in \beta \cap V_J$, we have $\dot s_{i_n} \cdot b \in \beta$, $\dot s_{i_{n-1}} \dot s_{i_n} \cdot b \in \beta$, \ldots, $\dot w \cdot b \in \beta$. 

By definition, \[\tag{b} u \cdot b \in \ensuremath{\mathbb {R}}\xspace_{>0} \dot w \cdot b+\sum_{b' \in \beta, \text{wt}(b')>\text{wt}(b), \text{wt}(b')-\text{wt}(b) \in \sum_{j=1}^n \ensuremath{\mathbb {N}}\xspace s_{i_1} \cdots s_{i_{j-1}} \alpha_{i_j}} \ensuremath{\mathbb {R}}\xspace_{\geqslant 0} b'.\] Since $w \in W^J$, $w(\Phi_J) \cap  \sum_{j=1}^n \ensuremath{\mathbb {N}}\xspace s_{i_1} \cdots s_{i_{j-1}} \alpha_{i_j}=\{0\}$. In other words, the only element in $\{\dot w \cdot b'; b' \in \beta \cap V_J\}$ that occurs in the right hand of (b) with positive coefficient is $\dot w \cdot b$.

Let $\sum_{b \in \beta \cap V_J} c_b b \in V_J$ with $u \cdot \sum_{b \in \beta \cap V_J} c_b b \in V_{\geqslant 0}$. Note that $$u \cdot \sum_{b \in \beta \cap V_J} c_b b=\sum_{b \in \beta \cap V_J} c_b u \cdot b \in \sum_{b \in \beta \cap V_J} c_b \ensuremath{\mathbb {R}}\xspace_{>0} \dot w \cdot b+\sum_{b' \in \beta, b' \notin \dot w \cdot V_J} \ensuremath{\mathbb {R}}\xspace_{\geqslant 0} b'.$$ Then $c_b \geqslant 0$ for all $b \in \beta \cap V_J$. Thus $\sum_{b \in \beta \cap V_J} c_b b \in (V_J)_{\geqslant 0}$. The Lemma is proved.
head: environment

label: prop:conj
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:conj}
Let $w_1, w_2 \in W$ with $\operatorname{supp}(w_2) \subset \operatorname{supp}(w_1)$. Then for any $g \in G_{w_1, w_2, >0}$ or $g \in G_{w_2, w_1, >0}$, conjecture \ref{conj} holds.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
We prove the case where $g \in G_{w_1, w_2, >0}$. The case $g \in G_{w_2, w_1, >0}$ is proved in the same way. 

Let $J_i=\operatorname{supp}(w_i)$. By Lemma \ref{lem:w-to-1}, there exists $u_1 \in U^-_{w_{J_2}, >0}$ such that $u_1 ^{-1} g u_1 \in t U^+_{w_1, >0}$ for some $t \in T_{>0}$ with $\alpha_i(t)>1$ for all $i \in J_2$. By Lemma \ref{lem:conj}, there exists $u_2 \in U^-_{w_{t, J_1} ^{-1}, >0}$ such that $u_2 ^{-1} u_1 ^{-1} g u_1 u_2 \in \bar t_{J_1} U^+_{w_1, >0}$. By definition, $w_{t, J_1} \in W_{J_1} \cap W^{J_2}$. Thus $\ell(w_{J_2} w_{t, J_1} ^{-1})=\ell(w_{J_2})+\ell(w_{t, J_1})$. We set $u_-=u_1 u_2 \in U^-_{w_{J_2} w_{t, J_1} ^{-1}, >0}$. It is also easy to see that there exists $u_+ \in L_{J_1} \cap U_{P^+_{I(\bar t_{J_1})}}$ such that 
\begin{itemize}
    \item the semisimple part $u_+ ^{-1} u_- ^{-1} g_s u_- u_+$ of $u_+ ^{-1} u_- ^{-1} g u_- u_+$ is $\bar t_{J_1}$;
    \item the unipotent part $u_+ ^{-1} u_- ^{-1} g_u u_- u_+$ of $u_+ ^{-1} u_- ^{-1} g u_- u_+$ is in $U^+_{\geqslant 0} \cap L_{I(\bar t_{J_1})}$. 
\end{itemize} 

Let $\bar t=\bar t_I$ and $J=I(\bar t)$. Let $w$ be the unique element in ${}^{J_1} W^J$ with $\bar t=\dot w ^{-1} \bar t_{J_1} \dot w$. Hence the semisimple part of $\dot w ^{-1} u_+ ^{-1} u_- ^{-1} g u_- u_+ \dot w$ is $\bar t$. Let $H=Z_G(g_s)$. Since $Z_G(\bar t)=L_J$, we have $H=(u_- u_+ \dot w) L_J (u_- u_+ \dot w) ^{-1}$. The pinning $\mathbf P_H$ of $H$ is defined to be the conjugate of the standard pinning of $L_J$ by the element $u_- u_+ \dot w$. In particular, $H_{\underline{\mathbf P_H}, \geqslant 0}=(u_- u_+ \dot w) L_{J, \geqslant 0} (u_- u_+ \dot w) ^{-1}$. 

Since $\bar t=\dot w ^{-1} \bar t_{J_1} \dot w$, we have $\Phi_{I(\bar t_{J_1})} =w(\Phi_{J}) \cap \Phi_{J_1}$. Since $w \in {}^{J_1} W^J$, we have $w ^{-1}(I(\bar t_{J_1})) \subset J$. Therefore $\dot w ^{-1} (U^+_{\geqslant 0} \cap L_{I(\bar t_{J_1})}) \dot w \subset U^+_{\geqslant 0} \cap L_J$. Thus $$g_u \in (u_- u_+) (U^+_{\geqslant 0} \cap L_{I(\bar t_{J_1})}) (u_- u_+) ^{-1} \subset (u_- u_+ \dot w) L_{J, \geqslant 0} (u_- u_+ \dot w) ^{-1}=H_{\underline{\mathbf P_H}, \geqslant 0}.$$ 

Part (1) of Conjecture \ref{conj} is proved. 

Let $V$ be an irreducible finite dimensional representation of $G$ and $v$ be a highest weight vector of $V$. Let $V_J \subset V$ be the $L_J$-submodule generated by $v$. Then $V(\bar t, c_M)=V_J$ and $V(g, c_M)=u_- u_+ \dot w \cdot V_J$. The nonnegative part $V(g, c_M)_{\underline{\mathbf P_H}, \geqslant 0}$ of $V(g, c_M)$ determined by the pinning $\mathbf P_H$ of $H$ equals $u_- u_+ \dot w \cdot V_{J, \geqslant 0}$. Since $\Phi_{I(\bar t_{J_1})}=w(\Phi_{J}) \cap \Phi_{J_1}$ and $w \in {}^{J_1} W$, we have $\dot w ^{-1} u_+ \dot w \in U_{P^+_J}$. Thus $u_- u_+ \dot w \cdot V_J=u_- \dot w u \cdot V_J=u_- \dot w \cdot V_J$ for some $u \in U_{P^+_J}$. Thus $$V(g, c_M)_{\underline{\mathbf P_H}, \geqslant 0}=u_- \dot w \cdot V_{J, \geqslant 0}.$$

By the proof of Lemma \ref{u-v}, $\dot w \cdot V_{J, \geqslant 0} \subset V_{\geqslant 0}$. Since $u_- \in U^-_{\geqslant 0}$, we have $u_- \cdot V_{\geqslant 0} \subset V_{\geqslant 0}$. Thus $V(g, c_M)_{\underline{\mathbf P_H}, \geqslant 0} \subset V_{\geqslant 0}$. 

On the other hand, let $\beta$ be the canonical basis of $V$. Suppose that $\sum_{b \in \beta \cap V_J} c_b b \in V_J$ with $u_- \dot w \cdot \sum_{b \in \beta \cap V_J} c_b b \in V_{\geqslant 0}$. By (b) in the proof of Lemma \ref{u-v}, we have $$u_- \dot w \cdot \sum_{b \in \beta \cap V_J} c_b b \in \sum_{b \in \beta \cap V_J} c_b \ensuremath{\mathbb {R}}\xspace_{>0} \dot w' \cdot b+\sum_{b' \in \beta, \beta' \notin \dot w' \cdot V_J} \ensuremath{\mathbb {R}}\xspace_{\geqslant 0} b'.$$ Thus $c_b \geqslant 0$ for all $b \in \beta \cap V_J$ and $\sum_{b \in \beta \cap V_J} c_b b \in (V_J)_{\geqslant 0}$. 

Therefore $V(g, c_M)_{\underline{\mathbf P_H}, \geqslant 0}=u_- \dot w \cdot V_{J, \geqslant 0}=u_- \dot w \cdot V_J \cap V_{\geqslant 0}=V(g, c_M) \cap V_{\geqslant 0}$. Part (2) of Conjecture \ref{conj} is proved.
head: environment
